opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because each of those on its own is hard, and the real challenge is that they tend to pull against each other. If you want higher resolution, that's more compute per frame. If you want longer memory, you need to condition on more context, which again costs compute. And if you want it to be real-time, you have a hard budget, you've got a fraction of a second to produce each frame while the user is actually interacting with it. So you can't just scale everything up and hope for the best.

The way we thought about it was really starting from the experience we wanted. With Genie 2, we had something that could generate pretty diverse interactive environments, but it wasn't real-time and the consistency would degrade after a short while. For Genie 3, we wanted it to feel like you're actually *in* a world: you can walk around, look away, come back, and things are still where you left them. That kind of persistence over a minute or so, at something like 720p and around 24 frames per second, was the bar we set for ourselves.

What's interesting is that memory in particular isn't something we hand-engineered. We don't have an explicit 3D representation or a map of the scene. The model is generating frame by frame, autoregressively, and the consistency emerges from it learning to attend back over what it's already generated. That's quite different from approaches that build explicit geometry, and it's part of why it can generalize across such a wide range of worlds, from photorealistic landscapes to fantastical, animated settings, because it's not constrained to things that fit neatly into a particular 3D format.

And then diversity really comes from the data and from scale. The broader the training distribution, the more the model learns general properties of how worlds behave, things like physics, lighting, how water moves, rather than memorizing specific environments.

So I'd say the challenge was less about solving any one of those dimensions and more about finding the point where they all come together well enough that the whole thing feels qualitatively different. And I think that's what we saw: once you hit real-time with reasonable memory and quality, it stops feeling like watching a generated video and starts feeling like a place you can explore. That opens up a lot, especially for us thinking about training embodied agents, where you want essentially unlimited, rich environments to learn in.

r001.rationale: The response says the goals pull against each other and describes setting a target, but does not say they must be pursued together from the outset.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Genie 3 with Genie 2, but does not characterize Genie 3 as effectively a new model despite keeping the Genie name.

r003.rationale: The response discusses memory, data, and scale, but does not describe specialists developing components while staying aware of the other components.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think the honest answer is that each of those things on its own is hard, and the real challenge was that they pull against each other. So if you take Genie 2, which came out at the end of 2024, that was a huge step for us in terms of diversity. You could prompt it with an image and get a playable 3D world, and it would generalize to lots of different environments. But it was slow, it was generating at a fairly low resolution, and you could only interact for maybe ten or twenty seconds before things started to drift. So we had a kind of existence proof that world models could do this, but not something you'd actually want to sit and play with, let alone train an agent in for extended periods.

The way I'd frame the shift for Genie 3 is that we stopped thinking about it as a video model with controls bolted on, and started thinking about it as a real-time system from the ground up. Once you commit to 24 frames a second at 720p, every architectural decision flows from that. You can't afford to do a lot of expensive iterative refinement per frame. You have to generate the next frame autoregressively, conditioned on the user's action, fast enough that it feels responsive, and that constraint ends up shaping everything else.

Memory is where it gets really interesting, because the naive thing is to say, well, just give it a longer context. But a longer context is exactly what you can't afford if you're trying to hit real-time. So a lot of the work was about how the model learns to maintain consistency over the course of a minute or more of interaction without us explicitly building in a 3D representation. We didn't want to hand it a NeRF or a Gaussian splat or an explicit map of the scene. We wanted it to emerge from the model learning to predict the world well. And what we found is that if you train at sufficient scale with the right objective, you get this emergent consistency where you can look away from something, come back, and it's still there. Someone paints on a wall, you turn around, you turn back, and the paint is still on the wall. That wasn't engineered in, which I think is the most exciting part.

And then diversity is almost the thing that holds the others together. If you had a model that was fast and consistent but only worked in a narrow set of environments, you'd basically have rebuilt a game engine the hard way. The whole point of the generative approach is that you can go from a photorealistic street to a cartoon to a historical setting with a text prompt, and the same system handles all of them. That generality is what makes it useful for training agents, because the agent can be exposed to an essentially unbounded curriculum of worlds.

So I'd say the challenge wasn't really solving four separate problems. It was finding the set of design choices where improving one didn't break the others, and then being quite disciplined about it. There were a lot of moments where we could have gotten better fidelity by giving up on real-time, or better memory by giving up on speed, and we had to resist that. The bet was that once you have all four together, the thing becomes qualitatively different. You can actually drop an agent in, or drop a person in, and the experience holds up, and that opens up a very different set of research questions than any of the pieces on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says the goals pull against each other and describes designing for real-time performance from the ground up, but it does not clearly state that pursuing all goals from the outset is what makes them achievable.

r002.rationale: It describes a major shift in Genie 3’s design, but does not characterize Genie 3 as effectively a new model despite retaining the Genie name.

r003.rationale: The response discusses balancing design choices across goals, but does not mention specialists developing individual components or their awareness of the other components.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that those things are all coupled. You want a world that looks compelling, but you also want it to respond immediately when you take an action. And you want that response to remain consistent with what you’ve already seen. If you turn around and come back, the world should still make sense.

Memory is particularly interesting because it’s more than maintaining the appearance of a scene. It’s also maintaining the consequences of your actions. And then diversity means you need that to work across many different environments, rather than building something that works beautifully in one narrow setting.

So I’d think about it as a systems problem as much as a modeling problem. Higher resolution and more context both put pressure on computation, while real-time interaction gives you a very tight budget. You have to develop those capabilities together and evaluate them together. Ultimately, the question is whether someone can interact with the world and feel that it’s coherent and responsive—not simply whether an individual frame looks good.

r001.rationale: The response says the capabilities are coupled and should be developed together, but does not state that pursuing them later makes the task harder or that the team must commit from the outset.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize Genie 3 as a new model or discuss its inherited name.

r003.rationale: The response mentions developing capabilities together, but does not identify specialists’ awareness of other components while developing their own.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that those capabilities are all coupled. You want a world that looks rich and detailed, but you also want it to respond immediately when you take an action. And you want that response to be consistent with what you’ve already seen. If you turn around and come back, the world should still make sense.

Memory is particularly interesting because it’s more than keeping the last few frames looking smooth. It’s about preserving the consequences of your actions and the structure of the environment over time. High resolution makes that more computationally demanding, and diversity means you need an approach that works across many different environments, rather than relying on assumptions about one particular world.

So I think about it as a systems problem as much as a modeling problem. You have to develop the model and the way you run it together, because real-time interaction is a hard constraint. A beautiful prediction that arrives too late doesn’t give you the experience of being in a world. The goal is to bring those pieces together so that you can explore, act, and feel that the environment is responding coherently.
